procedural_history.originating_court: High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh
procedural_history.impugned_order: Order dated 03.12.2021 of the High Court of Punjab & Haryana at Chandigarh in CRM-M No. 49115 of 2021, granting anticipatory bail to the respondent.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The High Court granted anticipatory bail to the respondent. The Supreme Court noted that the High Court's reasoning was contained in Paragraphs 7-12 of its order. The High Court failed to consider that the respondent was a declared proclaimed offender.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The State of Haryana appealed to the Supreme Court seeking cancellation of the anticipatory bail granted by the High Court. The Supreme Court allowed the appeal, effectively cancelling the anticipatory bail. The Supreme Court found that the High Court erred in brushing aside the fact that the respondent was a proclaimed offender.

directions: Pending applications stand consigned to records.

As far as the submission of the State is that the Impugned Order is the basis for co-accused to obtain anticipatory bail, it is for the State to take steps, if so advised, in accordance with law, in that behalf.
The respondent may seek regular bail which will be considered on its own merits without being prejudiced by the present judgment.

issue.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in granting anticipatory bail to the respondent, who was a proclaimed offender.

facts: The respondent had been declared a proclaimed offender on February 5, 2021.
In October 2021, while the proclamation was still in effect, the respondent applied for and was granted anticipatory bail by the High Court.
The High Court noted that it was not dealing with the validity of the proclamation proceedings but accepted the respondent's explanation for it based on his petition's averments.
The State appealed to the Supreme Court, seeking the cancellation of the anticipatory bail.
law: The grant of anticipatory bail under Section 438 of the Code of Criminal Procedure (CrPC) is a matter of judicial discretion.
As a general rule, established in cases like *Lavesh v State (NCT of Delhi)* and *State of Madhya Pradesh v Pradeep Sharma*, a proclaimed offender is not entitled to the benefit of anticipatory bail.
A person who is absconding and declared a proclaimed offender ordinarily deserves no concession or indulgence from the court.
An exception to this rule exists: in an "exceptional and rare case," the Supreme Court or High Courts, as Constitutional Courts, can consider granting anticipatory bail to a proclaimed offender.
application: The Supreme Court found that the High Court should not have entertained the respondent's application for anticipatory bail in the first place, given his status as a proclaimed offender.
It held that the respondent should have first successfully challenged the order declaring him a proclaimed offender before seeking pre-arrest bail.

The Court criticized the High Court for brushing aside the fact of the proclamation, which was subsisting when the bail was granted. The High Court's reasoning that the respondent was entitled to 'reform and course correct' was deemed incorrect in this context.

The Supreme Court determined that the present case did not present any "exceptional situation" that would justify departing from the general rule against granting anticipatory bail to a proclaimed offender.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court concluded that the High Court was incorrect in granting anticipatory bail to the respondent. It held that a proclaimed offender cannot seek anticipatory bail without first successfully challenging the proclamation order, except in rare and exceptional circumstances which were not present in this case. Therefore, the Supreme Court set aside the High Court's order and directed the respondent to surrender.

arguments.issue_text: Whether the High Court was correct in granting anticipatory bail to the respondent, who was a proclaimed offender.
appellant_arguments: Granting anticipatory bail was inappropriate given the nature of the allegations, the materials collected, and the fact that the respondent had been declared a proclaimed offender.
The respondent is the correctly identified person, and the allegations against him have been found to be true by the Investigation Agency.
respondent_arguments: The Investigating Agency has unnecessarily harassed and implicated the respondent, as evidenced by manipulations in the investigation records.
The State is targeting the respondent merely because he shares a common name with one of the accused.
The respondent's declaration as a proclaimed offender was not a result of him deliberately avoiding court.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A person who has been declared a proclaimed offender cannot seek anticipatory bail without first successfully challenging the order declaring them as such, except in rare and exceptional cases.
obiter: The grant of anticipatory bail, much like regular bail, is an exercise of judicial discretion where each case is determined by its own facts and merits.
General considerations for bail include the existence of a prima facie case against the accused and the nature and gravity of the accusation.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: In the facts and circumstances of the present case, it was not proper for the High Court to have granted anticipatory bail to the respondent.
legal_tests_applied: When considering bail, courts should assess factors including: '(i) whether there is any prima facie or reasonable ground to believe that the accused had committed the oﬀ ence; (ii) nature and gravity of the accusation; (iii) severity of the punishment in the event of conviction; (iv) danger of the accused absconding or ﬂ eeing, if released on bail; (vi) likelihood of the oﬀ ence being repeated; (vii) reasonable apprehension of the witnesses being inﬂ uenced; and (viii) danger, of course, of justice being thwarted by grant of bail.’
policy_considerations: The grant of bail should serve the larger public interest.
